contribution: Motion is described as position as a function of time: **position**, **displacement** $\Delta x = x_2 - x_1$ and **velocity** $v = \Delta x/\Delta t$ are vector quantities with a sign on a line, and the $(t, x)$ graph of uniform motion is a straight line whose slope is the velocity.
learn: describe motion as position as a function of time.
calculate displacement and velocity with their signs.
read the velocity of uniform motion from the slope of a graph of position against time.
prior: Velocity from lower secondary school: distance divided by time, $v = s/t$
Reading a coordinate system: axes, units and the steepness of a line

activities.text: A cyclist leaves home and rides at a uniform speed $2.0\,\text{km}$ along a straight road to the shop. She buys milk and rides straight back home. At the end the odometer shows $4.0\,\text{km}$, but a tracking app that measures the position from home shows $0\,\text{m}$. The app also draws a graph with time on the horizontal axis and the position of the cyclist on the vertical axis.
activities.question: What would such a graph look like, and what could be read from it about the cyclist's velocity and direction of travel?

activities.title: Review from lower secondary school
activities.prompt: A runner moves at a uniform speed $150\,\text{m}$ in $20\,\text{s}$. What is her velocity?

choices.feedback: You multiplied the distance and the time. Velocity tells how much distance is covered in a second, so the distance is divided by the time: $v = \dfrac{150\,\text{m}}{20\,\text{s}}$.

Correct: $v = \dfrac{150\,\text{m}}{20\,\text{s}} = 7.5\,\text{m/s}$. In this chapter the same idea gets a more exact form: the change in position takes the place of the distance, and the velocity gets a sign.
You divided the time by the distance. The result 0.13 is seconds per metre, not metres per second. Velocity is distance divided by time.
You subtracted the time from the distance, but different quantities cannot be subtracted from each other: metres and seconds are not the same unit. Velocity is a ratio $v = \dfrac{s}{t}$.

activities.title: Prediction 1: two different velocities
activities.prompt: Carts A and B start at the same time from the same point $x = 0$ and move in the positive direction at a uniform velocity. Cart B moves faster than A. What do the $(t, x)$ graphs of the carts look like?

choices.text: Both lines start from the origin, and the line of B rises less steeply than the line of A.
choices.feedback: A less steep line would mean that the position changes more slowly. In the values of the model B is at the position $40\,\text{m}$ at $10\,\text{s}$ and A at $20\,\text{m}$, so the position of B grows faster and its line is steeper.

choices.text: Both lines start from the origin, and the line of B rises more steeply than the line of A.
choices.feedback: The values of the model support this: both carts are at the position $0$ at the moment 0, but at $10\,\text{s}$ cart A is at the position $20\,\text{m}$ and cart B at $40\,\text{m}$. The velocity is the slope of the graph, so the faster cart gets the steeper line.

choices.text: Both lines start from the origin and are equally steep, because the carts start at the same time.
choices.feedback: A common starting point does not make the lines equally steep. The steepness is the slope, that is the velocity: in the values of the model B advances $4.0\,\text{m}$ per second and A $2.0\,\text{m}$ per second, so the lines move apart.

choices.text: Both lines start from the origin and are equally steep, but the line of B reaches higher.
choices.feedback: If the lines were equally steep, they would be at the same height at every moment. The line reaches higher precisely because it is steeper: the position of B grows faster than that of A.

activities.title: Prediction 2: a different starting position
activities.prompt: Cart A starts from the origin. Cart C starts from the position $x = 20\,\text{m}$ and moves in the same direction as fast as A. What happens to the positions and displacements of the carts as time passes?

choices.text: The displacement of C is greater than that of A, because the position of C is greater than that of A.
choices.feedback: In the values of the model each cart is displaced the same distance in $10\,\text{s}$: $20\,\text{m}$. Displacement is the change in position, and it does not depend on where the cart starts.

choices.text: The displacements of A and C are equal, and C stays $20\,\text{m}$ ahead all the time.
choices.feedback: The values of the model support this: A is displaced $20\,\text{m}$ and C is displaced $20\,\text{m}$, and the difference of the positions is $20\,\text{m}$ at every moment. Carts of equal velocity have equally steep, parallel lines; they differ only by the initial position $x_0$.

choices.text: The line of C rises more steeply than that of A, because C is farther from the origin.
choices.feedback: The steepness tells the velocity, not the starting position. In the values of the model the velocities of both are the same, so the lines are parallel: the starting position only moves the line of C higher.

choices.text: The position of C stays at 20 metres, because $20\,\text{m}$ is the starting position of C.
choices.feedback: In the values of the model the position of C grows every second. The number $20\,\text{m}$ is only the initial position; when the velocity is not zero, the position changes.

activities.title: Prediction 3: opposite directions
activities.prompt: Cart A starts from the origin and moves in the positive direction. Cart D starts from the position $x = 30\,\text{m}$ and moves towards the origin. What does the $(t, x)$ graph of D look like when it is drawn in the same coordinate system as the graph of A?

choices.text: The line of D rises towards the upper right, because velocity is always a positive number.
choices.feedback: In the values of the model the position of D decreases: at the moment 0 it is at $30\,\text{m}$ and at $10\,\text{s}$ at the position 0. When the position decreases, the graph falls. The sign of the velocity tells the direction, and a negative velocity is possible.

choices.text: The line of D falls towards the lower right and does not cross the line of A, because the carts move in different directions.
choices.feedback: Carts moving in different directions can be at the same position: in the values of the model A and D are both at the position $12\,\text{m}$ at $6\,\text{s}$. The intersection point of the graphs means precisely this meeting.

choices.text: The line of D falls towards the lower right and crosses the line of A, because D comes towards A.
choices.feedback: The values of the model support this: the position of D decreases from $30\,\text{m}$ to zero, the position of A grows from zero to $20\,\text{m}$, and they are at the same position at $6\,\text{s}$. A falling line means a negative velocity.

choices.text: The line of D is horizontal, because D is farther away and does not start moving straight away.
choices.feedback: In the values of the model the position of D changes right from the beginning. A horizontal line would mean that the position does not change, that is the cart would be at rest.

activities.text: In the simulation two carts move along a straight track, and their $(t, x)$ graph is drawn at the same time.
activities.howto: Press *Start* or drag the *Moment $t$* slider and watch what happens on the track and in the graph. Choose a *Case* and try how the graphs change. The direction and length of the arrow show the velocity, and the points on the track mark whole seconds. The line of the graph is drawn for the moments you have visited.
activities.model: The values are model values calculated by the simulation, not measurements of real carts. The carts move along a straight track at a constant velocity and are at full speed right away. Friction, acceleration and the size of the carts are ignored. The exception is case 4: cart $\text{E}$ moves forward for $4\,\text{s}$, stands still for $2\,\text{s}$ and returns for $4\,\text{s}$ at the same speed, so it ends up at its starting position.
activities.calc: The velocities are not given as numbers. Read the positions from the track, the clock or the graph and calculate the velocity as the ratio of the change in position to the change in time $v = \dfrac{\Delta x}{\Delta t}$. The distance $s$ is the length of the route travelled and the displacement $\Delta x$ is the change in position, so in case 4 $\Delta x = 0\,\text{m}$ even though $s \neq 0$.

activities.title: Experiment 1: two different velocities
activities.intro: Test prediction 1. The initial state selects case 1, where carts A and B start from the same point. Press *Start* and watch how the graphs are drawn. Then stop the clock by dragging the *Moment t* slider and record the positions at at least three different moments, for example $t = 0$, $t = 4.0\,\text{s}$ and $t = 10\,\text{s}$.

question.prompt: Calculate the velocity of cart B using two rows of the table. Give the answer in the unit m/s.
hints: Velocity is the change in position divided by the change in time. Choose two rows, for example the first and the last, and read the positions and times of B from them.
$v = \dfrac{\Delta x}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{x_2 - x_1}{t_2 - t_1}$. Use the numbers in the column $x_B$.
If the rows are $t = 0$ and $t = 10\,\text{s}$, then $v = \dfrac{x_B(10\,\text{s}) - x_B(0)}{10\,\text{s} - 0}$.

mistakes.feedback: This is the velocity of cart A. You used the column $x_A$, but the question was about cart B, whose column is $x_B$.
This is the position of B at $10\,\text{s}$. Velocity is calculated from the change in position $\Delta x$ divided by the change in time $\Delta t$, not from the position.

question.solution:
**Given:** positions of cart B from the table: $x_{1} = 0\,\text{m}$ at the moment $t_1 = 0$ and $x_{2} = 40\,\text{m}$ at the moment $t_2 = 10\,\text{s}$; the cart moves uniformly

**Find:** the velocity $v_\text{B}$ of cart B in the unit $\text{m/s}$

**Principle:** The motion of the cart is uniform, so the position changes by the same amount every second. Therefore any two rows of the table give the same velocity, and the velocity is the change in position divided by the change in time.

**Formula:** $v = \dfrac{\Delta x}{\Delta t}$, where $\Delta x = x_2 - x_1$ and $\Delta t = t_2 - t_1$. So $v = \dfrac{x_2 - x_1}{t_2 - t_1}$

**Conversions:** The positions are in metres and the times in seconds, so the result comes directly in the unit $\text{m/s}$. No conversions are needed.

**Substitution:** $v_\text{B} = \dfrac{40\,\text{m} - 0\,\text{m}}{10\,\text{s} - 0\,\text{s}} = 4.0\,\text{m/s}$

**Answer:** $4.0\,\text{m/s}$, two significant figures: the model values of the simulation are given with two figures, and the numbers $10\,\text{s}$ and $40\,\text{m}$ are given here with two figures.

**Reasonableness:** Cart B is faster than A ($2.0\,\text{m/s}$), and so its position grows faster in the table. Another pair of rows gives the same result: for example at $t = 4.0\,\text{s}$ B is at the position $16\,\text{m}$, and $\dfrac{16\,\text{m}}{4.0\,\text{s}} = 4.0\,\text{m/s}$. The velocity is positive, because the position grows.

activities.title: Experiment 2: a different starting position
activities.intro: Test prediction 2. The initial state selects case 2, where cart C starts ahead of A. Press *Start* and look at the graphs. Then record the positions at at least three different moments, for example $t = 0$, $t = 4.0\,\text{s}$ and $t = 10\,\text{s}$, and calculate the change in position of each cart between the rows.

question.prompt: Calculate the velocity of each cart from the table. What do you notice?

choices.text: The velocity of C is greater than that of A, because the position $x$ of C is greater than that of A.
choices.feedback: Compare the changes in position, not the positions: each cart advances the same amount in every time interval of equal length. The position tells where the cart is, and the velocity tells how fast the position changes.

choices.text: The velocity of both is $2.0\,\text{m/s}$: the velocity depends on the change in position, not on the position.
choices.feedback: Correct. For example between the rows $t = 0$ and $t = 10\,\text{s}$ $\Delta x = 20\,\text{m}$ for both and $v = \dfrac{20\,\text{m}}{10\,\text{s}} = 2.0\,\text{m/s}$. In the graphs this shows as parallel lines: the same slope, a different initial position $x_0$.

choices.text: The velocities of the carts are $20\,\text{m/s}$ and $0$, because C starts $20\,\text{m}$ away from the origin.
choices.feedback: The initial position is not a velocity. When you calculate the change in position and divide by the time, the same number comes out for both. The starting position shows only as the point where the line crosses the position axis.

choices.text: The velocity of A is greater than that of C, because A has to go farther than C.
choices.feedback: Velocity does not depend on how far the cart should go. In the table the position of both grows $20\,\text{m}$ in $10\,\text{s}$, so the velocities are the same and A does not get closer to C.

activities.title: Experiment 3: opposite directions
activities.intro: Test prediction 3. The initial state selects case 3, where cart D moves towards the origin. Press *Start* and watch where the graphs cross. Record the positions at at least three different moments, for example $t = 0$, $t = 6.0\,\text{s}$ and $t = 10\,\text{s}$.

question.prompt: Calculate the velocity of cart D using two rows of the table. Give the answer with its sign in the unit m/s.
hints: Read the positions of D from two rows and calculate the change in position, final position minus initial position. In which direction does the position change?
$v = \dfrac{x_2 - x_1}{t_2 - t_1}$, and $x_2 - x_1$ is negative when the position decreases.

mistakes.feedback: The magnitude is correct, but the sign is missing. The position of D decreases, so $\Delta x < 0$ and the velocity is negative: D moves in the negative direction of the $x$-axis.
This is the initial position of D. The velocity is obtained when the change in position $\Delta x$ is divided by the change in time $\Delta t$.

question.solution:
**Given:** positions of cart D from the table: $x_1 = 30\,\text{m}$ at the moment $t_1 = 0$ and $x_2 = 0\,\text{m}$ at the moment $t_2 = 10\,\text{s}$; the cart moves uniformly

**Find:** the velocity $v_\text{D}$ of cart D with its sign in the unit $\text{m/s}$

**Principle:** The motion is uniform, so the velocity is the change in position divided by the change in time. The change is calculated as final minus initial, so the sign tells the direction: when the position decreases, the velocity is negative.

**Formula:** $v = \dfrac{\Delta x}{\Delta t}$, where $\Delta x = x_2 - x_1$ and $\Delta t = t_2 - t_1$. So $v = \dfrac{x_2 - x_1}{t_2 - t_1}$

**Conversions:** The positions are in metres and the times in seconds, so no conversions are needed. Do not swap the initial and final positions, because then the sign would be reversed.

**Substitution:** $v_\text{D} = \dfrac{0\,\text{m} - 30\,\text{m}}{10\,\text{s} - 0\,\text{s}} = \dfrac{-30\,\text{m}}{10\,\text{s}} = -3.0\,\text{m/s}$

**Answer:** $-3.0\,\text{m/s}$, two significant figures: the model values of the simulation are given with two figures, and the numbers $30\,\text{m}$ and $10\,\text{s}$ are given here with two figures.

**Reasonableness:** Cart D moves towards the origin, so the position decreases and the velocity must be negative. Check backwards: $30\,\text{m} + (-3.0\,\text{m/s}) \cdot 10\,\text{s} = 0\,\text{m}$, which is the final position in the table. The speed is $3.0\,\text{m/s}$, and it is a positive number even though the velocity is negative.

activities.title: Measurement data: a robot moves along a line
activities.text: A robot moves along a straight line at a uniform velocity. A distance sensor measures its position $x$ every two seconds. Every measurement has a small error, so the points do not lie exactly on one line. Here the measurements are given as a table and as a $(t, x)$ graph (example data, not a real experiment). | $t$ (s) | $x$ (m) | |---|---| | 0 | 4.2 | | 2 | 6.8 | | 4 | 10.2 | | 6 | 13.3 | | 8 | 15.8 | | 10 | 19.1 | A line fitted through the points has been drawn in the figure so that the points lie roughly evenly on both sides of it. The fitted line starts from the position $x_0 = 4.1\,\text{m}$, that is from the point $(0\,\text{s};\, 4.1\,\text{m})$.

question.prompt: Choose another point on the fitted line far from the starting point $(0\,\text{s};\, 4.1\,\text{m})$ and read its $t$ and $x$ from the graph. Calculate the slope of the line, that is the velocity of the robot, using these two points. Give the answer in the unit m/s.
hints: The line does not pass through all the measured points, so read the point from the line, not from the table. Choose a point that is far from the starting point, for example near the moment $t = 10\,\text{s}$, and record its t and x.
$v = \dfrac{\Delta x}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{x_2 - x_1}{t_2 - t_1}$. The starting point is $(0\,\text{s};\, 4.1\,\text{m})$; the line ends at about the position $19\,\text{m}$.
Between the moments $t = 0$ and $t = 10\,\text{s}$ the position of the line grows by about $19\,\text{m} - 4\,\text{m} = 15\,\text{m}$.

mistakes.feedback: You divided the last position by the time: $\dfrac{19\,\text{m}}{10\,\text{s}}$. The line does not start from the origin but from the position of about $4\,\text{m}$, so the change in position must be used: $\Delta x = 19\,\text{m} - 4.1\,\text{m}$.

You calculated the velocity from two neighbouring measured points. The error of each of them has a relatively large effect, because the interval is short. Choose points on the line far from each other, and the errors become smaller.
You divided the change in time by the change in position. Velocity is the change in position divided by the change in time, $v = \dfrac{\Delta x}{\Delta t}$.

question.solution:
**Given:** the starting point of the fitted line $(t_1;\, x_1) = (0\,\text{s};\, 4.1\,\text{m})$ and a second point far from it read from the graph $(t_2;\, x_2) \approx (10\,\text{s};\, 19\,\text{m})$; the robot moves at a uniform velocity

**Find:** the slope of the line, that is the velocity $v$ of the robot, in the unit $\text{m/s}$

**Principle:** The robot moves at a uniform velocity, so its $(t, x)$ graph is a straight line, and the slope of the line is the velocity. The measured points have a small error, so the velocity is calculated from points on the fitted line and not from individual measurements.

**Reading the graph:** The starting point $(0\,\text{s};\, 4.1\,\text{m})$ is given. The second point is read at the moment $t = 10\,\text{s}$, at the right edge of the graph: from this point go up to the line and from there to the left to the $x$-axis. The line is a little below the $20\,\text{m}$ grid line, so we read $x_2 \approx 19\,\text{m}$. The point is thus read between the grid lines $15\,\text{m}$ and $20\,\text{m}$. The interval between the grid lines is $5\,\text{m}$, so the value can be read to about a metre. For points far apart this error is small compared with the change. The vertical rise is $x_2 - x_1$ and the horizontal run is $t_2 - t_1$.

**Formula:** $v = \dfrac{\Delta x}{\Delta t}$, where $\Delta x = x_2 - x_1$ and $\Delta t = t_2 - t_1$. So $v = \dfrac{x_2 - x_1}{t_2 - t_1}$

**Conversions:** The positions are in metres and the times in seconds, so no conversions are needed. The initial position $4.1\,\text{m}$ is not zero, but it cancels in the difference.

**Substitution:** $v = \dfrac{19\,\text{m} - 4.1\,\text{m}}{10\,\text{s} - 0\,\text{s}} = \dfrac{14.9\,\text{m}}{10\,\text{s}} \approx 1.5\,\text{m/s}$

**Answer:** $1.5\,\text{m/s}$, two significant figures, because the position $19\,\text{m}$ read from the graph is accurate only to about a metre, so $\Delta x \approx 15\,\text{m}$ is a two-figure number. The scatter of the measured points also limits the accuracy: the slope of the least-squares line is $1.49 \pm 0.03\,\text{m/s}$.

**Reasonableness:** The line rises, so the velocity is positive. The equation of position of the line is about $x = 4.1\,\text{m} + 1.5\,\text{m/s} \cdot t$, and at the moment $t = 10\,\text{s}$ it gives $19.1\,\text{m}$, which agrees with the value read, $19\,\text{m}$. The average velocity between the first and last measurement in the table is $\dfrac{19.1\,\text{m} - 4.2\,\text{m}}{10\,\text{s}} = 1.49\,\text{m/s}$, and in two seconds the position grows by about $1.5\,\text{m/s} \cdot 2\,\text{s} = 3\,\text{m}$, as between the rows of the table, so the result fits the measurements. Dividing by the final position alone would wrongly give $1.9\,\text{m/s}$.

activities.title: Back-and-forth motion
activities.text: Cart E is in case 4 of the simulation. It moves $4.0\,\text{s}$ in the positive direction, stands still for $2.0\,\text{s}$ and moves $4.0\,\text{s}$ back at the same speed. The speed during the motion is $2.0\,\text{m/s}$. Its $(t, x)$ graph is below. You can repeat the motion in the simulation by choosing case 4. The cart ends up at its starting position, and the distance travelled is $16\,\text{m}$.

question.prompt: What is the average velocity of cart E over the whole $10\,\text{s}$?

choices.text: $1.6\,\text{m/s}$, because the cart travelled $16\,\text{m}$ in $10\,\text{s}$.
choices.feedback: The number $16\,\text{m}$ is the distance travelled. The average velocity is calculated from the displacement: $v_\text{avg} = \dfrac{\Delta x}{\Delta t}$. The distance gives the average speed (distance travelled divided by time), and here it is $1.6\,\text{m/s}$.

choices.text: $0$, because the displacement is $\Delta x = 0\,\text{m} - 0\,\text{m} = 0$.
choices.feedback: Correct. At the end the cart is at the same position as at the beginning, so $\Delta x = 0$ and $v_\text{avg} = \dfrac{0}{10\,\text{s}} = 0$. The distance was still $16\,\text{m}$: displacement and distance are different quantities.

choices.text: $2.0\,\text{m/s}$, because that was the velocity of the cart during the motion.
choices.feedback: During the motion the velocity was $+2.0\,\text{m/s}$, but the average velocity over the whole time also takes into account standing still and the return. Calculate $\Delta x$ for the whole time interval.

choices.text: $-2.0\,\text{m/s}$, because the velocity of the last part was negative.
choices.feedback: The velocity of the last part was $-2.0\,\text{m/s}$, but the average velocity over the whole time is calculated from the whole displacement. The initial and final positions are the same, so the displacement is zero.

activities.title: Return to your predictions
activities.prompt: Compare your predictions with the tables and graphs. What did you find out about the steepness of a line, the initial position and the sign of the velocity? Also return to the cyclist at the beginning: why is her displacement zero even though the distance is $4.0\,\text{km}$?

activities.title: Find the error
activities.prompt: A student calculates the velocity of a cart. At the moment $t = 2.0\,\text{s}$ the cart is at the position $30\,\text{m}$ and at the moment $t = 8.0\,\text{s}$ at the position $12\,\text{m}$. She writes $v = \dfrac{30\,\text{m} - 12\,\text{m}}{8.0\,\text{s} - 2.0\,\text{s}} = 3.0\,\text{m/s}$. Where is the error?

choices.text: The positions were subtracted the wrong way round: $\Delta x = 12\,\text{m} - 30\,\text{m} = -18\,\text{m}$, so $v = -3.0\,\text{m/s}$.
choices.feedback: Correct. The position decreases, so the cart moves in the negative direction and its velocity is negative. The student subtracted the positions the wrong way round and lost the sign.

choices.text: The times were subtracted the wrong way round: $\Delta t$ should be calculated as $2.0\,\text{s} - 8.0\,\text{s}$ and not the other way round.
choices.feedback: Time moves forward, so $\Delta t = t_2 - t_1 = 6.0\,\text{s}$ is positive. The error is in the calculation of the displacement.

choices.text: Velocity is always positive, so the result $+3.0\,\text{m/s}$ is correct and there is no error in the calculation.
choices.feedback: Velocity is a vector quantity, and the sign tells the direction. A negative velocity means motion in the negative direction of the $x$-axis, and here the position really does decrease.

choices.text: The unit should be metres and not metres per second, because the calculation has only positions and times.
choices.feedback: A change in position divided by time is metres per second. The unit m/s is correct; the error is in the sign of the result.

activities.title: Apply to a new situation
activities.prompt: A sled slides down a straight slope at a uniform velocity. On the slope there is a marker post at which the position is 0. At the moment $t = 3.0\,\text{s}$ the sled is at the position $4.0\,\text{m}$ and at the moment $t = 7.0\,\text{s}$ at the position $24\,\text{m}$. At what position is the sled at the moment $t = 10.0\,\text{s}$? Give the answer in metres.
hints: First find the velocity using the two given moments.
The velocity is $v = \dfrac{x_2 - x_1}{t_2 - t_1}$. After that, the later position is the position at one moment plus the velocity times the elapsed time: $x = x_2 + v\,\Delta t$.
$v = \dfrac{24\,\text{m} - 4.0\,\text{m}}{7.0\,\text{s} - 3.0\,\text{s}}$, and the extra time from the moment $7.0\,\text{s}$ to the moment $10.0\,\text{s}$ is $3.0\,\text{s}$.

mistakes.feedback: You calculated $x = v\,t$, that is you assumed that the sled was at the position 0 at the moment 0. From the given points it can be seen that the initial position is about $-11\,\text{m}$. Use a known point and add only the time that has passed since then.

You added the effect of the whole time $10.0\,\text{s}$ to the position $24\,\text{m}$. The position $24\,\text{m}$ is at the moment $7.0\,\text{s}$, so the extra time is only $10.0\,\text{s} - 7.0\,\text{s} = 3.0\,\text{s}$.
This is the velocity of the sled. The question was about the position at the moment $10.0\,\text{s}$, so you still have to use the velocity to calculate how much the position changes.

activities.solution:
**Given:** positions of the sled: $x_1 = 4.0\,\text{m}$ at the moment $t_1 = 3.0\,\text{s}$ and $x_2 = 24\,\text{m}$ at the moment $t_2 = 7.0\,\text{s}$; the moment asked for $t = 10.0\,\text{s}$; the velocity is uniform

**Find:** the position $x$ of the sled at the moment $t = 10.0\,\text{s}$ in metres

**Principle:** The sled slides at a uniform velocity, so its velocity is obtained from two known points and its position at a later moment from a known point using the velocity and the elapsed time. The position at the starting moment is not zero, so $v\,t$ alone is not valid.

**Formula:** $v = \dfrac{x_2 - x_1}{t_2 - t_1}$ and $x = x_2 + v\,(t - t_2)$. Substituting the first into the second gives $x = x_2 + \dfrac{x_2 - x_1}{t_2 - t_1}\,(t - t_2)$

**Conversions:** The positions are in metres and the times in seconds, so no conversions are needed. The change in time is calculated as a difference, not from the moment $t = 0$.

**Substitution:** $v = \dfrac{24\,\text{m} - 4.0\,\text{m}}{7.0\,\text{s} - 3.0\,\text{s}} = \dfrac{20\,\text{m}}{4.0\,\text{s}} = 5.0\,\text{m/s}$ and $x = 24\,\text{m} + 5.0\,\text{m/s} \cdot (10.0\,\text{s} - 7.0\,\text{s}) = 24\,\text{m} + 15\,\text{m} = 39\,\text{m}$

**Answer:** $39\,\text{m}$, two significant figures like the positions $4.0\,\text{m}$ and $24\,\text{m}$.

**Reasonableness:** The sled moves in the positive direction, so the position must be greater than $24\,\text{m}$. Another route: the initial position is $x_0 = 4.0\,\text{m} - 5.0\,\text{m/s} \cdot 3.0\,\text{s} = -11\,\text{m}$, and $x = -11\,\text{m} + 5.0\,\text{m/s} \cdot 10.0\,\text{s} = 39\,\text{m}$, the same result. The velocity $5.0\,\text{m/s}$ is $18\,\text{km/h}$, which fits a sled sliding down a slope.

activities.text: Practise further on three levels. The tasks of level 1 use one formula, and level 3 requires reasoning. Level 1 is enough for the basic skills; levels 2 and 3 are optional and more advanced, so do them if level 1 goes well. Draw the $(t, x)$ graph in your notebook whenever it helps.

activities.title: 1. Concept
activities.prompt: The $(t, x)$ graph of a cart is a straight line that falls from left to right and crosses the $t$-axis (that is the point $x = 0$) at the moment $t = 8\,\text{s}$. What does this tell about the cart?

choices.text: The cart moves in the negative direction and passes the origin at the moment $8\,\text{s}$.
choices.feedback: Correct. A falling line means that the position decreases, that is the velocity is negative. Crossing the $t$-axis means that the position is then zero.

choices.text: The cart stops at the origin at the moment $8\,\text{s}$ and stays there.
choices.feedback: Stopping would show as a horizontal part of the graph, where the position does not change. Here the line continues falling also after the crossing point.

choices.text: The cart moves in the positive direction and its speed decreases all the time.
choices.feedback: A positive velocity would give a rising line. Also, a straight line means uniform motion, where the velocity does not change.

choices.text: The cart is at rest before the moment $8\,\text{s}$ and starts from the origin only then.
choices.feedback: The graph tells the position at every moment, also before the moment $8\,\text{s}$. So the cart is already moving earlier, and at the moment $8\,\text{s}$ its position is 0.

activities.title: 2. Calculation
activities.prompt: At the moment $t = 0$ a cart is at the position $-12\,\text{m}$ and moves uniformly at a velocity $2.5\,\text{m/s}$ in the positive direction. At what position is the cart at the moment $t = 10\,\text{s}$? Give the answer in metres with its sign.
hints: The position is the initial position plus the displacement. What is the displacement in $10\,\text{s}$?
Use the formula $x = x_0 + v\,t$. The initial position is negative.

mistakes.feedback: You calculated only the displacement $v\,t = 25\,\text{m}$. The position is obtained when the displacement is added to the initial position, which is $-12\,\text{m}$.
You added the number $12\,\text{m}$ of the initial position as positive. The initial position is negative, so $x = -12\,\text{m} + 25\,\text{m}$.

activities.solution:
**Given:** $x_0 = -12\,\text{m}$ at the moment $t = 0$, $v = 2.5\,\text{m/s}$ in the positive direction, the moment asked for $t = 10\,\text{s}$

**Find:** the position $x$ of the cart at the moment $t = 10\,\text{s}$ with its sign in metres

**Principle:** The motion of the cart is uniform, so the position changes by the product of the velocity and the time. The position is the initial position plus this displacement, and the initial position is negative, so its sign must be taken into account.

**Formula:** $x = x_0 + v\,t$. The formula is already solved for the position: $x = x_0 + v\,t$

**Conversions:** The position is in metres, the velocity in the unit $\text{m/s}$ and the time in seconds, so no conversions are needed.

**Substitution:** $x = -12\,\text{m} + 2.5\,\text{m/s} \cdot 10\,\text{s} = -12\,\text{m} + 25\,\text{m} = 13\,\text{m}$

**Answer:** $13\,\text{m}$, two significant figures, because the velocity $2.5\,\text{m/s}$ and the time $10\,\text{s}$ have two figures and the sum $-12\,\text{m} + 25\,\text{m}$ is to the accuracy of a metre.

**Reasonableness:** The cart is displaced $25\,\text{m}$ forward, which is more than the initial distance from the origin ($12\,\text{m}$), so it passes the origin and the position is positive. The cart is at the origin at the moment $\dfrac{12\,\text{m}}{2.5\,\text{m/s}} = 4.8\,\text{s}$, so at the moment $10\,\text{s}$ it has passed the origin and travelled another $5.2\,\text{s} \cdot 2.5\,\text{m/s} = 13\,\text{m}$.

activities.title: 3. Explain
activities.prompt: Explain in your own words why the distance travelled by a cyclist can be $4.0\,\text{km}$ but the displacement zero, and how the magnitude and direction of the velocity can be seen from a $(t, x)$ graph. Use the concepts position, displacement and velocity.
criteria: I say that the displacement is the change in position, final position minus initial position, and that it is zero when the final position is the same as the initial position.
I say that the distance is the length of the route and does not depend on the direction.
I say that the velocity is the slope of the graph $\dfrac{\Delta x}{\Delta t}$: the steepness tells the magnitude and rising or falling the direction.
I use the units correctly: position and displacement in metres, velocity in metres per second.
activities.model: The cyclist rides $2.0\,\text{km}$ to the shop and back, so the length of the route, that is the distance, is $4.0\,\text{km}$. The displacement $\Delta x = x_2 - x_1$, however, is the change in position from the initial position to the final position. The final position is the same as the initial position, so $\Delta x = 0$. In the $(t, x)$ graph the velocity is the slope of the line $v = \dfrac{\Delta x}{\Delta t}$: the steeper the line, the greater the magnitude of the velocity. A rising line means a positive velocity and a falling line a negative one. In the cyclist's graph there is a rising part on the way to the shop and a falling part on the way back.

activities.text: Finally, three quick questions. Answer first yourself and only then open the answer.
